blocks.text: Manhattan distance measures how far apart two points are if you can only travel along a grid, horizontal and vertical moves only, never a diagonal shortcut. It is named after the block-based street layout of Manhattan, where a taxi has to drive around blocks rather than cutting straight through them.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What Manhattan Distance Measures

Where Euclidean distance measures the straight line gap between two points, Manhattan distance measures the total distance traveled moving only along the axes, first across, then up, or any combination of grid-aligned steps that adds up to the same total.

blocks.alt: Manhattan distance travels only along grid lines
blocks.caption: No diagonal shortcut, only horizontal and vertical segments

blocks.text: The alternate name taxicab distance comes from exactly this picture: a taxi cannot drive diagonally through a city block, it can only follow the streets, so its total driving distance between two intersections is the Manhattan distance between them, not the Euclidean one.

This restriction to grid-aligned movement is not a limitation to work around, in many real problems it is the accurate description of how movement or difference actually works, which is exactly what makes Manhattan distance the correct, not just convenient, choice in those settings.
2. The Formula

Manhattan distance sums the absolute value of the difference along every dimension, d = absolute(x2 minus x1) plus absolute(y2 minus y1), extended to as many dimensions as needed. Unlike Euclidean distance, nothing gets squared or square rooted, only added directly.

code.content:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([4, 6])
dist = np.sum(np.abs(a - b))
print(dist)   # 7, since |4-1| + |6-2| = 3 + 4 = 7

blocks.text: The absolute value step is essential here, without it a positive gap in one dimension could cancel out a negative gap in another, producing a total that understates how far apart the two points actually are.
Because nothing is squared, every term contributes to the total in direct proportion to its size, a linear relationship that differs meaningfully from how squared terms grow in the Euclidean formula.
3. Manhattan vs Euclidean: A Direct Comparison

For the same two points, Manhattan distance is always greater than or equal to Euclidean distance, since the straight line path from the Euclidean distance lesson can never be longer than any grid-restricted path between the same two points.
The two measures only agree exactly when the two points differ along a single dimension, as the second row shows, since there is no diagonal to shortcut through in that case.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Notice the gap between the two measures grows as the point moves further off the axes, at (1,1) the ratio is already about 1.41, and this gap continues to widen in higher dimensions, which is part of why the two measures can disagree more sharply as dimensionality increases.

blocks.text: 4. Manhattan Distance in Code
Just like Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance vectorizes cleanly and works identically regardless of how many dimensions are involved.

code.content:
a = np.random.rand(50)
b = np.random.rand(50)
dist = np.sum(np.abs(a - b))   # works for any number of dimensions
from scipy.spatial.distance import cityblock
print(cityblock(a, b))   # same result, using the library name for Manhattan distance

blocks.text: The scipy name cityblock is simply another synonym for the same measure, alongside Manhattan and taxicab, all three names describe the identical calculation.
5. Why It Is Also Called L1 Distance

The magnitude and norm lesson covered the ordinary vector length as one specific way of measuring size, technically called the L2 norm. Manhattan distance corresponds to a different norm entirely, the L1 norm, which sums absolute values instead of squaring and square rooting them. Manhattan distance is simply the L1 norm applied to the difference between two points, the exact same relationship Euclidean distance has with the L2 norm.

code.content:
diff = b - a
l1_distance = np.sum(np.abs(diff))          # Manhattan / L1
l2_distance = np.sqrt(np.sum(diff ** 2))     # Euclidean / L2
print(l1_distance, l2_distance)

blocks.text: Naming distance measures after their underlying norm, L1 for Manhattan and L2 for Euclidean, is standard practice throughout machine learning libraries, so recognizing this pattern early makes reading unfamiliar documentation considerably faster.
6. Robustness to Outliers

Because Euclidean distance squares every difference, a single dimension with an unusually large gap dominates the total distance disproportionately. Manhattan distance, using plain absolute values instead of squares, weighs every dimension gap more evenly, which makes it noticeably less sensitive to a single extreme outlier dimension.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Two points differing by 1 in nine dimensions and by 20 in a tenth dimension: the Euclidean distance is dominated almost entirely by that one dimension, since 20 squared is 400, versus 1 squared nine times totaling only 9. The Manhattan distance instead adds 20 directly alongside the nine 1s, giving that outlying dimension proportionally less overwhelming influence on the total.

blocks.text: This robustness advantage is not free, in datasets where large gaps genuinely reflect meaningful differences rather than noise, dampening their influence with Manhattan distance can actually throw away useful signal, which is why the choice between the two measures deserves real thought rather than a fixed default.
7. Manhattan Distance and Sparsity

The same L1 idea that defines Manhattan distance also shows up prominently in machine learning as L1 regularization, used in Lasso regression, which adds the sum of absolute values of model weights as a penalty during training. This penalty has a distinctive effect: it tends to push many weights all the way to exactly zero, producing a sparse model that effectively performs feature selection on its own.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
model = Lasso(alpha=0.1)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.coef_)   # many entries often come out as exactly 0.0

blocks.text: This sparsity-inducing behavior is a direct geometric consequence of the L1 norm shape, and it is one of the main reasons Manhattan distance and L1 regularization keep appearing together throughout applied machine learning.

This is in sharp contrast to L2, or Ridge, regularization, which shrinks weights toward zero smoothly but rarely forces any of them to land exactly on zero, a distinction worth remembering whenever choosing between the two penalty types for a given model.
8. Manhattan Distance in AI Practice

items: K nearest neighbor classifiers can be configured to use Manhattan distance instead of Euclidean, often preferred for high dimensional or sparse feature data such as text represented as word counts.
Grid-based pathfinding problems, such as robot navigation restricted to horizontal and vertical moves, use Manhattan distance directly as a natural, exact measure of movement cost.
Lasso regression, mentioned in section 7, uses the L1 penalty to encourage simpler, more interpretable models with fewer active features.

Manhattan distance is sometimes preferred over Euclidean distance in very high dimensional spaces specifically because it is less affected by the curse of dimensionality effect covered later in this module.

blocks.text: Choosing which distance measure a k-NN classifier should use is often decided empirically, by comparing validation accuracy under Manhattan versus Euclidean distance rather than by theory alone, since the better choice genuinely depends on how the specific dataset is shaped.
9. The Broader Minkowski Family

Chebyshev distance, the extreme case as p grows very large, is used in practice for problems like king moves on a chessboard, where the cost of a move is determined entirely by whichever single axis requires the most steps, horizontal or vertical, not by their sum.
9.1 Manhattan and Euclidean as Two Special Cases

Manhattan distance and Euclidean distance are both special cases of a broader family called the Minkowski distance, parameterized by a number p: raise every difference to the power p, sum them, then take the p-th root. Setting p to 1 gives Manhattan distance exactly, and setting p to 2 gives Euclidean distance exactly.

Higher values of p push the formula to weigh the single largest dimension gap even more heavily, in the limit approaching a measure called Chebyshev distance that considers only the single largest dimension difference and ignores every other dimension entirely.

Setting p below 1 is technically possible but breaks several convenient mathematical properties a proper distance measure is expected to have, which is why p is almost always kept at 1 or above in practice.
10. The Shape of a Manhattan Distance Ball

One vivid way to see the difference between Manhattan and Euclidean distance is to draw every point that sits exactly distance 1 away from the origin under each measure. Under Euclidean distance, that set of points forms a perfect circle. Under Manhattan distance, the same set of points forms a diamond, a square rotated 45 degrees.

blocks.alt: Points at distance 1 from the origin
blocks.caption: Euclidean gives a circle, Manhattan gives a diamond, both centered on the same origin

blocks.text: This picture explains section 6 directly: the diamond shape reaches its corners along the axes and pulls inward along the diagonals, meaning any single dominant dimension contributes to the boundary more gently than the circle does.

Every point on the diamond boundary satisfies the same equation, absolute x plus absolute y equals 1, a direct visual proof of the Manhattan distance formula from section 2 applied specifically to points exactly 1 unit from the origin.
11. Manhattan Distance with Sparse and Text Data

Text represented as word count vectors, where most entries are 0 and only a handful of words actually appear in a given document, is a classic case where Manhattan distance is often preferred over Euclidean. Since most dimensions are already 0 in both vectors being compared, the sum of absolute differences reduces cleanly to counting how the nonzero word counts actually differ, without the extra squaring step doing much additional work.

code.content:
doc1 = np.array([2, 0, 1, 0, 3])   # word counts for document 1
doc2 = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 3])   # word counts for document 2
print(np.sum(np.abs(doc1 - doc2)))   # 2, a simple, interpretable count of total word-count disagreement

blocks.text: This same reasoning extends to any high dimensional, mostly-zero feature representation, one-hot encoded categorical variables being a particularly common example throughout applied machine learning pipelines.
12. Manhattan Distance and Median-Based Clustering

The k-means algorithm, covered in the Euclidean distance lesson, updates each cluster center to the mean of its assigned points, which is the natural choice when minimizing total Euclidean distance. A variant called k-medians instead updates each cluster center to the median of its assigned points, which is the natural choice when minimizing total Manhattan distance, and inherits the same outlier robustness advantage covered in section 6.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A cluster containing the values 1, 2, 3, 4, and 100 has a mean of 22, dragged far from where most of the points actually sit, but a median of 3, squarely in the middle of the typical values. K-medians, built around Manhattan distance, naturally resists this kind of outlier distortion the way k-means, built around Euclidean distance, does not.

blocks.text: Choosing between k-means and k-medians in practice often comes down to whether the dataset is expected to contain extreme outliers, exactly the same tradeoff between Euclidean and Manhattan distance covered back in section 6.
13. A Worked Example
Compute both the Manhattan and Euclidean distance between the points (2, 3, 1) and (5, 7, 1), reusing the same points from the Euclidean distance lesson worked example.

code.content:
a = np.array([2, 3, 1])
b = np.array([5, 7, 1])
manhattan = np.sum(np.abs(a - b))
euclidean = np.linalg.norm(a - b)
print(manhattan, euclidean)   # 7 5.0

blocks.text: Manhattan distance sums the absolute differences directly to 7, while Euclidean distance takes the square root of the sum of squares to reach 5, confirming Manhattan distance is always at least as large, as established in section 3.

This same pair of points, reused directly from the Euclidean distance lesson worked example, makes the two lessons easy to compare side by side and confirms both formulas were applied correctly against a shared, already-verified answer.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming Manhattan and Euclidean distance always give proportionally similar rankings, they can disagree on which of two candidate points is closer, especially in higher dimensions.
Forgetting the absolute value in the formula and accidentally summing signed differences, which can partially cancel out and produce a meaninglessly small result.
Applying Manhattan distance where the underlying real world movement genuinely allows diagonal shortcuts, mismatching the distance measure to the actual geometry of the problem.

Confusing Manhattan distance with the L1 norm of a single vector, they are the same formula, but the norm measures a vector length from the origin while distance measures the gap between two arbitrary points.

blocks.text: It is also worth remembering that Manhattan distance is not automatically the safer or more correct choice just because it is more outlier robust, some problems genuinely have a diagonal, straight-line notion of closeness that Manhattan distance would misrepresent.
15. Practice: Compute Both Distances
Take the points (0, 0) and (3, 4), already familiar from the Euclidean distance lesson, and compute the Manhattan distance between them.

code.content:
a = np.array([0, 0])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.sum(np.abs(a - b)))   # 7

items: Comparing this result, 7, against the Euclidean distance of exactly 5 for the same two points reinforces the always-greater-or-equal relationship covered in section 3.

blocks.text: Now compute the Manhattan distance for the points (0, 0) and (5, 0) as well, and notice it comes out equal to the Euclidean distance for that pair, exactly the single-dimension agreement case noted in section 3.
Key Takeaway

The diamond-shaped unit ball from section 10 is worth keeping as a mental image whenever choosing between distance measures, it makes the outlier robustness from section 6 and the sparsity connection from section 7 feel like the same underlying geometric fact rather than two separate coincidences.

Manhattan distance sums the absolute differences across every dimension, corresponding to travel restricted to grid lines rather than a direct diagonal path. It is always at least as large as Euclidean distance for the same two points, more robust to a single extreme outlier dimension, and closely tied to L1 regularization and the sparse, feature-selecting behavior that comes with it.

Together with Euclidean distance from the previous lesson, and cosine similarity and cosine distance immediately ahead, Manhattan distance rounds out the standard toolkit for measuring how close or how far apart two points or vectors are, each suited to a different kind of data and a different notion of closeness.

Choosing between Manhattan, Euclidean, or one of the other Minkowski family members from section 9 is rarely a purely mathematical decision, it depends on what kind of movement, error, or difference actually makes sense for the data and task at hand.
